H1.text: A coconut falls from a tall tree and lands hard. A hammer, lifted high, drives a nail.

H2.text: Nobody pushed them down. So where did that energy come from?

H3.text: Diya opens the tap on the ground floor. The water tank sits up on the roof.

H4.text: Nobody is pushing the water, yet it gushes out fast. What is the water carrying?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will measure it in joules.

P1.text: So what is gravitational potential energy?

P2.text: Lift a book onto a high shelf. Your arms do work against gravity.

P3.text: That work is not lost. It is stored in the book, because of its height.

P4.text: Let it fall, and gravity gives the energy back, as motion.

P5.text: Energy stored because of height is called gravitational potential energy, U.

S1.text: Let's run it. A two kilogram ball, lifted slowly by a rope.

S2.text: To lift it slowly, the rope pulls up with nineteen point six newtons. That is just its weight, m g.

S3.text: One metre up, the rope has done nineteen point six joules of work.

S4.text: Every metre adds the same nineteen point six joules. At five metres, U is ninety eight joules.

S5.text: On the graph, U against height is a straight line. Double the height, double the energy.

S6.text: Now let it go. The stored energy turns into speed.

S8.text: The weight still points down, and the speed keeps growing. Gravity hands back the stored energy.

D1.text: Now the formula, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. To lift it slowly, the upward force F must equal the weight, m g.

D3.text: Step two. Force and movement both point up. So the work is force times height. W equals m g h.

D4.text: Step three. That work is stored. U equals m g h, taking the ground as zero.

D5.text: Step four. Units. Kilograms, times metres per second squared, times metres. Joules.

D6.text: Step five. Going up, gravity does minus m g h of work. U is the work done against gravity.

T1.text: Remember this. U equals m g h, where h is the height above the level you call zero.

R1.text: But height above what? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. Diya's tank sits twelve metres above the ground.

R3.text: Two. From the ground, one kilogram of its water has a U of about one hundred and eighteen joules.

R4.text: Three. From the first floor, four metres up, the same water has only seventy eight joules.

R5.text: Four. Water in the sump, two metres below the ground, has a negative U. About minus twenty joules.

R6.text: We choose the zero. What matters is how much U changes.

C2.text: Same two kilogram ball. Lift it twice as high, and U doubles.

C3.text: Same height. Use a ball twice as heavy, and U doubles again.

C4.text: Now you try. A one kilogram ball on a four metre shelf, or a two kilogram ball on a two metre shelf. Which stores more U? Pause and decide.

C5.text: Neither! m times h is four in both. Each one stores thirty nine point two joules.

C6.text: One more. A satellite is lifted two thousand kilometres above the Earth. Can we still use m g h? Pause and think.

C7.text: No! Up there, g is only about five point seven. m g h works only for heights small next to Earth's radius.

W2.text: Diya's pump lifts five hundred litres of water from the sump, two metres below the ground, to the tank, twelve metres up. How much energy is stored?

W3.text: One litre of water has a mass of one kilogram. So m is five hundred kilograms.

W4.text: The water climbs two metres, then twelve more. The height gained is fourteen metres.

W5.text: Change in U is m g times the height gained. Five hundred, times nine point eight, times fourteen.

W6.text: That is sixty eight thousand six hundred joules. The water carries it down to Diya's tap.

X2.text: A box is pushed five metres up a ramp, at thirty degrees. Many students take h as five metres.

X3.text: But h is the height climbed, straight up. Five times sine thirty is two point five metres. Only the climb counts.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In short numericals on the change in U, and inside bigger energy problems.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A five kilogram box goes from the floor to a shelf two point five metres high. Take a one metre table top as zero, and g as ten. Find U on the floor and on the shelf. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Minus fifty joules, and plus seventy five joules.

A2.text: The floor is one metre below the zero. Five times ten times minus one. Minus fifty.

A3.text: The shelf is one point five metres above the zero. Five times ten times one point five. Plus seventy five.

A4.text: The change is still one hundred and twenty five joules. Only the zero moved.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Where does the water from a rooftop tank get its energy?

Y3.text: Two. How can potential energy be negative?

Y4.text: Three. Why can we not use m g h for a satellite, far above the Earth?

N1.text: Next time: a steep path and a winding road up the same hill. Does gravity care which one you took? Find out in conservative and non-conservative forces.
